summary: Defines DOTS signal channel configuration parameters that peers can negotiate to use the CoAP Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 options. These allow faster, more robust transfer of large amounts of data, which helps during DDoS attacks when packets may be lost.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road is jammed, you send a big load as small boxes that can each be resent if lost, instead of one huge truck that must start over.

questions: how to send large data during a ddos attack
coap q-block1 and q-block2 with dots
how does dots send large data during a ddos attack
subtitle: Lets DOTS peers negotiate the tuning knobs for sending big messages quickly while a DDoS attack drops packets.

tldr.problem: DOTS peers must exchange large messages while a DDoS attack may be dropping packets, but the standard CoAP block-wise options send one block at a time and rely on acknowledgements that may never get through.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9362 adds six optional configuration attributes to the DOTS signal channel (max-payloads, non-max-retransmit, non-timeout, non-receive-timeout, non-probing-wait, non-partial-timeout) so peers can negotiate the parameters of the Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 options, and it defines a YANG module and CBOR keys for them.
tldr.outcome: DOTS clients and servers can tune robust block transmission using the same negotiation procedure they already use for other signal channel parameters, with no new vulnerabilities beyond those of DOTS and CoAP.

today: RFC 9362 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9132 and RFC 9177.

sections.title: Why Block Transfer Needs Tuning
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) runs over UDP. Its Block1 and Block2 options, from RFC 7959, split data that does not fit in one IP packet into blocks. They work well when there is little or no packet loss, but they are synchronous: each block must be requested, and the next one can only be asked for or sent once the previous one has completed. Block rates are therefore controlled by round-trip times.

That is a poor fit for a network under a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack, where responses may be dropped in only one direction. RFC 7959 recommends Confirmable responses to cope with loss, but in a flooded-pipe situation the returning ACK packets may not get through. RFC 9177 defines the Q-Block1 and Q-Block2 options for applications such as DOTS that cannot use Confirmable responses, and it adds guards so that a CoAP agent does not overload the network.

The gap this document fills: RFC 9132 lets DOTS peers negotiate transmission parameters such as PROBING_RATE, but it does not cover the extra congestion control parameters that RFC 9177 introduces. RFC 9362 adds signal channel attributes for them.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal block sending is like passing one note at a time and waiting for a thank-you before the next. That is slow when the mail room is flooded, so the sides need a way to agree on a faster, sturdier routine.

sections.title: The Congestion Control Parameters
sections.content:
Section 7.2 of RFC 9177 defines the parameters that guard against aggressive sending. RFC 9362 describes each one and gives the defaults shown in its Table 1.

  • MAX_PAYLOADS (default 10): the maximum number of payloads that can be transmitted at any one time.
  • NON_MAX_RETRANSMIT (default 4): the maximum number of times a request to retransmit missing payloads can occur without a response from the remote peer.
  • NON_TIMEOUT (default 2 s): the maximum delay between sending sets of MAX_PAYLOADS payloads for the same body.
  • NON_TIMEOUT_RANDOM (between 2 and 3 s): the initial actual delay between sending the first two sets of the same body.
  • NON_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT (default 4 s): the maximum time to wait for a missing payload before requesting retransmission, by default twice NON_TIMEOUT.
  • NON_PROBING_WAIT (between 247 and 248 s): limits the wait needed when using PROBING_RATE.
  • NON_PARTIAL_TIMEOUT (247 s): used for expiring partially received bodies.

These work together with PROBING_RATE, which in CoAP is the average data rate that must not be exceeded when sending to a peer that does not respond. The whole body of blocks is subject to PROBING_RATE, not the individual packets. If the wait between bodies exceeds NON_PROBING_WAIT, the wait is capped at that value.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the rules of a careful sender: how many boxes to send at once, how long to wait before asking about a missing one, and when to give up on a half-finished delivery.

sections.title: The New Signal Channel Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 9362 augments the ietf-dots-signal-channel YANG module from RFC 9132 with six attributes, each of which echoes one of the parameters above: max-payloads, non-max-retransmit, non-timeout, non-receive-timeout, non-probing-wait and non-partial-timeout. All are optional. Time-valued attributes are expressed in seconds.

Defaults differ slightly from plain CoAP in places. non-max-retransmit defaults to max-retransmit, and the text notes that DOTS uses 3 rather than the 4 CoAP uses generically. non-timeout defaults to ack-timeout, non-receive-timeout defaults to twice non-timeout, and non-partial-timeout defaults to 247 seconds.

If max-payloads is supplied in both idle-config and mitigating-config, the two values MUST be the same. If it appears in only one of them, the other MUST be updated to the same value.

DOTS clients negotiate, configure and retrieve these values using the procedure in Section 4.5 of RFC 9132. Two implementation notes apply: non-probing-wait should keep some jitter rather than be hard-coded, and when any session configuration parameter changes, non-probing-wait and non-partial-timeout should be recalculated per RFC 9177 unless explicit values were negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides already chat about their settings. This document just adds six more settings to that chat, all optional, so each side can say what it prefers.

sections.title: The YANG Module and Tree
sections.content:
The module is named ietf-dots-robust-trans and uses the data structure extension from RFC 8791. It augments both the mitigating-config and idle-config parts of the signal channel configuration.

Each attribute is a container holding a current-value (or current-value-decimal for the time-based ones). A direction choice with a server-to-client-only case adds max-value and min-value, which appear only in messages from the server to the client and tell the client the acceptable range. Integer attributes use uint16; time attributes use decimal64 with two fraction digits and the unit seconds.

Section 5 of RFC 9132 says the module is not meant to be used via NETCONF or RESTCONF. It serves as an abstract representation of what is carried in DOTS signal channel messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A YANG module is a tidy form that says exactly what each setting is called and what kind of value it holds, so both sides read it the same way.

sections.title: Encoding and a Worked Example
sections.content:
On the wire, the messages are CBOR. Each new container is mapped to a CBOR key of major type 5 (a map): max-payloads is 32776, non-max-retransmit 32777, non-timeout 32778, non-receive-timeout 32779, non-probing-wait 32780 and non-partial-timeout 32781. Implementers must check that their YANG-to-CBOR encoder output matches the RFC's table.

The RFC shows a CoAP PUT to .well-known/dots/config/sid=123 with content format application/dots+cbor. It sets a non-default max-payloads of 15 in both idle and mitigating configuration, and leaves non-max-retransmit, non-timeout and non-receive-timeout at their defaults. Because non-probing-wait and non-partial-timeout are not given, they are computed by the algorithms in RFC 9177. The example is written in JSON for readability, following the mapping tables of RFC 9132.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new setting gets a number label so it can be sent in a compact form. The example shows one side asking to send 15 boxes at a time and keeping everything else normal.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of the DOTS signal channel are in Section 11 of RFC 9132, and CoAP-specific ones are in Section 11 of RFC 9177. RFC 9362 states that its module does not introduce any new vulnerabilities beyond those.

For IANA, the six CBOR keys (32776 to 32781) are registered in the DOTS Signal Channel CBOR Key Values registry, with the IESG as change controller. IANA has also registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-dots-robust-trans and the YANG module ietf-dots-robust-trans with prefix dots-robust.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding these settings does not open any new doors for attackers. The numbers and names were also written into the official public lists so nobody else reuses them.
